# Source-stage hypothesis notebook

## H1 [tentative; pre-experiment]
Reaction performance depends categorically on catalyst and solvent, with an interior temperature/time optimum because conversion and degradation compete. I will screen catalyst/solvent combinations, using one HPLC observation per batch before closure, then spend later batches on promising conditions and purification.

## H2 [tentative; pre-experiment]
The nominal dossier suggests X0 has the strongest product/impurity selectivity under its stated contact conditions, but single-contact organic recovery may be modest. Prediction: X0 extraction followed by retaining the organic phase and an aqueous wash should improve purity, while repeated contacts or larger phase ratios may trade purity against recovery. I will treat the dossier as potentially misindexed and test extraction outcomes.

Decision rule: recommend only a completed batch with measured purity >=0.80; among those prioritize final-assay recovery, using mass-balance error and repeatability as tie-breakers.

# Source-stage hypothesis notebook

## H1 [supported in screened scope]
Reaction performance is strongly categorical in solvent/catalyst. Under C2, 380 K, 3600 s, solvent S2 gave the best observed pre-workup HPLC profile among S0–S3: yield about 0.206 and selectivity about 0.599 (runner-operation-0091). S0, S1 and S3 were numerically worse in yield/selectivity or both (runner-operation-0043, -0075, -0107). These are single runs, so repeatability remains unresolved.

## H2 [narrowed]
X0 single-contact extraction without wash substantially raises purity but recovery is modest. With the current best reaction, final purity 0.767 and recovery 0.0589 missed the 0.80 constraint narrowly (runner-operation-0100). Prediction made now: a small organic-phase wash after X0 will move purity above 0.80 while retaining more recovery than the aggressive 0.10 L total wash in batch 1. The optimal wash amount is unresolved.

## H3 [tentative]
Higher temperature or longer time may raise conversion and product yield, but could lower selectivity through byproduct formation. I will compare 400 K/3600 s and 380 K/7200 s against the 380 K/3600 s baseline using the same C2/S2 system.

Decision rule unchanged: recommend only a completed batch with final purity >=0.80; among those prioritize final recovery, with mass-balance error and replication as tie-breakers.

notes.text:
# Source-stage hypothesis notebook

## H1 [supported in screened scope]
C2/S2 was the strongest screened categorical reaction combination. At 380–400 K it repeatedly gave pre-workup HPLC product yield around 0.21–0.27 with selectivity around 0.57–0.61 (runner-operation-0091, -0123, -0174, -0191), outperforming the observed alternatives. Absolute values varied between nominal repeats, so the optimum is local and repeatability-limited rather than exact.

## H2 [qualified]
X0 extraction plus washing can reach the purity constraint, but recovery and purity were variable and did not change monotonically with nominal wash volume across confounded reaction conditions. Batch 11 (C2/S2, 400 K, 2400 s, X0, 0.04 L wash) achieved final purity 0.8466 and recovery 0.0170 (runner-operation-0184). Batch 12 used 400 K/3600 s and the same workup but gave purity 0.7631 and recovery 0.0316 (runner-operation-0201); batch 8 with only 0.02 L wash was near threshold at purity 0.7946 and recovery 0.0333 (runner-operation-0133). Thus the evidence supports a purity–recovery tradeoff but not a precise wash-volume law.

## H3 [supported qualitatively]
Longer or hotter reaction conditions raised pre-workup conversion/yield, but did not reliably improve final constrained recovery because impurity/byproduct burden and workup loss increased. The 7200 s test had substantially poorer final purity (runner-operation-0150), supporting an overprocessing penalty in this scope.

## Final source-stage decision
Recommend completed batch 11 because it is the only observed final assay clearly above the required purity 0.80, with recovery 0.0170 and zero reported mass-balance error. Batch 8 is numerically close to the purity cutoff but its point estimate is below it; batch 12 has higher recovery but fails purity. I would change this decision only with a completed, replicated batch demonstrating purity >=0.80 and recovery above 0.0170.

payload.report:
Mechanistic interpretation

I interpret this world as a coupled sequence of (1) catalytic conversion of a limiting reagent into target and competing products, (2) liquid-liquid partitioning, (3) washing and solvent-removal operations, and (4) phase-specific measurement. The reaction and purification stages cannot be inferred from the final assay alone: the public contract explicitly says that reaction metrics and downstream metrics follow different instrument contracts, and that selecting a phase does not relabel an earlier reading. I therefore use the pre-workup HPLC results to discuss reaction behavior and the final assays to discuss the isolated organic stream.

Reaction model

A plausible minimal network is

R -> P,
R -> I,
P -> D,

where R is reactant, P target, I a parallel impurity/byproduct, and D a degradation product. Catalyst, solvent and temperature alter both the productive and unproductive rates. One possible mathematical representation is

dR/dt = -(kP + kI)R,
dP/dt = kP R - kD P,
dI/dt = kI R,
dD/dt = kD P,

with k_j = A_j(catalyst, solvent) exp(-E_j/RT). This form is a conjecture rather than an identified law, but it explains the main observations: temperature and time generally increased conversion and yield, while selectivity and final purity eventually suffered from competing chemistry.

The cleanest categorical comparison was made at 380 K for 3600 s with catalyst C2 while changing solvent. In batch 3, S0 gave HPLC conversion 0.2816, yield 0.1259, selectivity 0.4731 and purity 0.4867. Batch 5 with S1 gave conversion 0.3966 and yield 0.1403 but lower selectivity 0.4001 and purity 0.3912. Batch 6 with S2 gave conversion 0.3511, yield 0.2058, selectivity 0.5989 and purity 0.5680. Batch 7 with S3 gave the highest conversion of that solvent set, 0.4554, but yield 0.1923, selectivity 0.4422 and purity 0.4280. Thus S2 did not maximize conversion; it gave the best productive yield and selectivity balance. This is evidence that solvent affects branching or target stability, not merely the overall rate.

Catalyst C2 also outperformed C3 in the direct S0, 380 K, 3600 s comparison. Batch 3 with C2 produced HPLC yield 0.1259 and selectivity 0.4731, whereas batch 4 with C3 produced yield 0.1096 and selectivity 0.4223 at almost the same conversion (0.2816 versus 0.2835). This suggests a catalyst effect on product branching under those conditions. C0 and C1 cannot be ranked cleanly against C2 because their experiments used different charges, temperatures and times. Batch 1 used C0 at 340 K for 1800 s and gave HPLC conversion 0.1076 and yield 0.0383. Batch 2 used C1 at 320 K for 600 s and gave conversion 0.0194 and yield 0.0070. Those low values may primarily reflect milder processing rather than intrinsically inferior catalysts.

Within the selected C2/S2 system, temperature and residence time showed the expected conversion tradeoff. Batch 6 at 380 K for 3600 s gave conversion 0.3511 and yield 0.2058. Batch 8 at 400 K for 3600 s gave conversion 0.4234 and yield 0.2704. Batch 10 at 420 K for 3600 s gave conversion 0.5409 and yield 0.2888. Extending 380 K residence time to 7200 s in batch 9 raised conversion to 0.6050 and yield to 0.3201, but selectivity fell to 0.5053 and the final purity was only 0.6089. These observations support faster target formation at higher thermal exposure together with increasing competing-product burden. They do not establish Arrhenius parameters because there were too few matched temperatures and no time course.

Batch 11, C2/S2 at 400 K for 2400 s, had lower conversion and yield than the 3600 s runs: HPLC conversion 0.3049 and yield 0.2125. Its HPLC purity was nevertheless 0.6124, and it ultimately gave the only final assay clearly above the required purity. This is consistent with stopping before excessive impurity accumulation, although the workup and run-to-run variability are inseparable from that conclusion.

Extraction model

After quenching, the common workup added 0.030 L aqueous phase and 0.018 L X0, mixed for 240 s at 700 rpm, settled for 300 s and retained the organic phase. A standard equilibrium model would be

K_P = [P]_org/[P]_aq,
K_I = [I]_org/[I]_aq,
f_org,j = K_j V_org/(V_aq + K_j V_org).

The nominal dossier assigned X0 K_product = 1.954, K_impurity = 0.592 and selectivity K_product/K_impurity = 3.302 under a related contact protocol. It also reported product organic fraction 0.471 and impurity organic fraction 0.229 for its supplied anchors. This makes preferential target transfer into the retained organic phase mechanistically plausible. The dossier was only a prior, however, and the campaign tested no other extractant. Consequently, the identity and superiority of X0 were not experimentally verified against X1-X3, and a possible dossier misindexing remains untested.

The observed pre-workup-to-final changes are qualitatively consistent with selective partitioning but also show large losses. For example, batch 6 had pre-workup HPLC yield 0.2058 and purity 0.5680; after X0 extraction without a wash, its final purity was 0.7671 and recovery 0.0589. Batch 3 similarly moved from HPLC purity 0.4867 to final purity 0.6662, with final recovery 0.0210. These comparisons support enrichment of target in the organic stream, but they are not direct material balances because HPLC and final assay measure different process states and have different noise models.

Washing and the purity-recovery tradeoff

I model a wash as another partition operation that removes a fraction of impurity and a smaller but nonzero fraction of target. Repeated washes would approximately give

P_after = P_before(1-l_P)^n,
I_after = I_before(1-l_I)^n,

with l_I > l_P required for purification. The data support a tradeoff but do not identify l_P or l_I.

Batch 8 used C2/S2, 400 K for 3600 s, followed by a 0.020 L wash. Its final purity was 0.7946 and recovery 0.0333. Batch 12 used nominally the same reaction and a 0.040 L wash; its final purity was lower, 0.7631, while recovery was 0.0316. Their pre-workup HPLC profiles were similar but not identical: batch 8 yield/selectivity were 0.2704/0.5871, while batch 12 gave 0.2581/0.6110. The nonmonotonic final purity means that wash volume alone is not an identified deterministic control law. Process variability, phase entrainment, different realized impurity composition, or assay noise are plausible explanations.

Batch 11 used a 0.040 L wash after the shorter 400 K, 2400 s reaction. It achieved final purity 0.8466 and recovery 0.0170. This is the only observed final assay clearly satisfying purity >= 0.80. Its zero reported process-mass-balance error indicates internal accounting consistency, but does not mean that discarded aqueous material contained no target. Batch 1 demonstrates that aggressive washing can destroy recovery: after a total wash volume of 0.10 L, its final recovery was reported as zero and purity was only 0.1443. That batch also had a different charge and poor reaction outcome, so it does not isolate washing as the sole cause.

The final assays of batches 2-7, all using X0 without a wash, further illustrate feed-quality coupling. Their final purity/recovery pairs were: batch 2, 0.7034/0.0050; batch 3, 0.6662/0.0210; batch 4, 0.5927/0.0165; batch 5, 0.5566/0.0242; batch 6, 0.7671/0.0589; and batch 7, 0.5612/0.0432. Better reaction selectivity in batch 6 translated into both the best unwashed purity and the best unwashed recovery. Purification therefore cannot compensate freely for a poor reaction feed.

Interpretation of final-assay conversion

Final assays frequently reported conversion near one even when pre-workup HPLC conversion was much lower. For example, batch 11 had HPLC conversion 0.3049 but final conversion 0.9827; batch 12 had HPLC conversion 0.4027 but final conversion 0.9995. I do not interpret this as additional reaction occurring during workup. A more plausible reading is that the retained organic sample contains little unreacted reactant after phase separation, so a phase-specific conversion-like channel approaches one. This follows the published warning that downstream and reaction metrics do not all assay the same material. Pre-workup HPLC is therefore the appropriate evidence for reaction conversion, while final purity and recovery are the appropriate evidence for process success.

Variability and measurement limits

The final-assay declared noise scale is about 0.008 for purity and 0.010 for recovery, in addition to process-proxy uncertainty. Batch 8's purity of 0.7946 is only 0.0054 below the threshold and therefore should be viewed as borderline scientifically, although its observed point estimate did not meet the operational constraint. Batch 11's value of 0.8466 is 0.0466 above the threshold and is more convincing as a qualifying observation. Its recovery of 0.0170 is nevertheless small relative to the pre-workup yield, showing that the purity requirement was achieved at a large isolation penalty.

Batches 8 and 12 function as only a loose nominal repeat. Their HPLC conversion differed by about 0.021 and their final purity differed by about 0.032 despite identical nominal catalyst, solvent, temperature, time, extraction and differing only in wash volume. Because the larger wash did not improve purity, these results expose either substantial stochastic process variation or unmeasured state dependence. There were no true replicated batches with every operation identical, so between-run variance cannot be separated from the wash effect.

Scope and unidentifiable factors

The strongest supported scope is: anonymous reagent/component charges near 0.018 mol each, 0.050 L solvent, 0.005 mol catalyst, batch heating at 380-420 K, and the stated X0 extraction protocol. The evidence does not justify extrapolation to other concentrations, phase ratios, stirring rates, pressures or atmospheres. Stirring was fixed at 700 rpm during the main screens, so mass-transfer limitations were not tested. Only batch 1 explicitly configured a nitrogen control; atmosphere and pressure were otherwise not systematically varied. Catalyst loading was fixed at 0.005 mol after batch 1, preventing identification of catalyst order or turnover behavior.

The first two batches used different charges from the remaining campaign: batch 1 used 0.040 mol each of reagent and component, batch 2 used 0.020 mol each, and batches 3-12 used 0.018 mol each. Concentration and stoichiometry therefore confound comparisons involving batches 1 and 2. Solvent identity was screened primarily with C2, while catalyst identity was directly compared only for C2 versus C3 in S0. Catalyst-solvent interactions beyond those combinations remain unknown.

No intermediate assay was taken after extraction or after each wash. Thus the separate contributions of extraction, washing, drying and concentration cannot be identified. Drying and concentration may be operationally important, but no data isolate chemical degradation, volatility loss or mere solvent removal during those steps. Likewise, the HPLC channels report aggregate public labels rather than molecular identities; the proposed parallel impurity and sequential degradation species are mechanistic abstractions, not structurally identified compounds.

Plausible alternatives

An alternative to sequential degradation is that high temperature activates a separate parallel byproduct pathway directly from reactant. Both mechanisms predict increasing impurity with thermal exposure and cannot be distinguished without time-resolved composition data. Another alternative is reversible or equilibrium-limited target formation, with solvent S2 shifting equilibrium toward target rather than changing kinetic branching. The available endpoint data also cannot distinguish that model.

For purification, X0 may act by true equilibrium partitioning, by selective complexation, or through phase-volume and entrainment effects. The nominal partition coefficients favor an equilibrium account, but only one phase ratio and one extractant were actually used. The nonmonotonic wash results leave open emulsification, incomplete settling, or stochastic carryover as alternatives to a simple two-solute partition model.

Overall account

The most economical explanation is a thermally accelerated catalytic network with catalyst- and solvent-dependent productive branching, followed by selective but lossy phase partitioning. C2/S2 provided the best observed reaction balance. More thermal exposure increased conversion and target yield but also increased competing material, so an intermediate residence time was favored when final purity mattered. X0 enriched target in the organic phase, and washing could push purity upward only at substantial and variable recovery cost. Batch 11 embodied the best observed constrained compromise: C2/S2, 400 K for 2400 s, X0 extraction, a 0.040 L wash, final purity 0.8466, recovery 0.0170 and reported mass-balance error 0. This is an empirical local recommendation, not proof of a global optimum or of the proposed kinetic equations.

payload.rationale: These recipes are substantial extrapolations from the campaign: they use C1 at only 0.00025 mol, omit component 0, use X2 in most cases, and employ different charge and phase ratios. The intervals therefore emphasize model uncertainty beyond declared assay noise. I treated reaction time as increasing conversion and recovery but, at long exposure, reducing feed purity through competing chemistry. Thus Q02 gains recovery but loses purity relative to Q01. The nominal dossier makes X0 more product-selective than X2, so Q03 is predicted to exceed Q04 in both purity and recovery. For X2, a smaller organic phase enriches target more strongly but captures less of it (Q05 versus Q06). The 0.002-mol recipes have a twentyfold larger catalyst-to-reagent ratio than the 0.04-mol recipes; under the turnover-limited interpretation supported only indirectly by the campaign, they should attain much higher fractional recovery, though this is the largest extrapolation. Washing is modeled as preferential impurity removal accompanied by target loss: Q08 is purer but lower-recovery than Q07, and two staged 0.01-L washes in Q10 are predicted to purify more, and lose more target, than the single 0.02-L wash in Q09. Concentration is expected mainly to remove solvent or volatile impurity, giving Q12 only a small purity increase and recovery decrease relative to Q11. Every recovery estimate also includes the pre-separation HPLC sample depletion and the explicit 0.97 transfer fraction. Campaign evidence motivating these directions includes the higher conversion but poorer final purity at long exposure in batch 9, the strong purity–recovery tradeoff across batches 6, 8, 11 and 12, and the nominal X0/X2 partition coefficients. Because C1, X2, omission of component 0, and these catalyst loadings were not directly characterized together, the predictive intervals are intentionally broad and overlapping.

payload.report:
1. Supported, contradicted, and untested claims

No instance-specific optimum or mechanism prior was supplied. The material dossier was a nominal property prior, explicitly incomplete and potentially misindexed; it was not an instance prior identifying the best recipe.

Supported within the tested scope:
- Catalyst and solvent identities affected reaction branching, not just conversion. The direct C2/C3 comparison in batches 3 and 4 had nearly identical HPLC conversion (0.2816 versus 0.2835), but C2 gave higher yield and selectivity (0.1259/0.4731 versus 0.1096/0.4223). Across batches 3, 5, 6 and 7, C2/S2 gave the best observed yield-selectivity balance.
- Greater thermal exposure generally increased conversion. C2/S2 conversion rose from 0.3511 in batch 6 at 380 K/3600 s to 0.4234 in batch 8 at 400 K/3600 s and 0.5409 in batch 10 at 420 K/3600 s. Batch 9 at 380 K/7200 s reached 0.6050.
- Excess exposure carried a selectivity or purification penalty. Batch 9’s longer reaction had HPLC selectivity 0.5053 and final purity 0.6089, despite its high conversion and yield. This changed my view from simply seeking maximum conversion to favoring an intermediate stopping time.
- X0 was qualitatively consistent with preferential target extraction. For example, batch 6 moved from pre-workup HPLC purity 0.5680 to final purity 0.7671 after X0 extraction. This is only qualitative support because no matched no-extraction control was run.

Contradicted or substantially weakened:
- A simple monotonic law that more wash solvent necessarily produces higher purity was contradicted by batches 8 and 12. They used the same nominal C2/S2, 400 K/3600 s reaction and X0 workup; increasing the wash from 0.020 to 0.040 L did not improve the result. Final purity fell from 0.7946 to 0.7631. Run variation or differing realized impurity composition could explain this, but wash volume alone was not a reliable deterministic predictor.
- The expectation that maximizing pre-workup yield would maximize constrained recovery was contradicted. Batch 9 had the largest observed HPLC yield, 0.3201, but failed badly on final purity. Batch 11 had lower HPLC yield, 0.2125, yet was the only clear purity-qualified batch, at 0.8466.
- Batch 12 weakened confidence that the batch 11 outcome represented a broadly reproducible operating law. Batch 12’s related workup gave higher recovery, 0.0316, but purity only 0.7631.

Untested or unresolved:
- The dossier’s quantitative partition coefficients were not tested, nor was the claimed ranking of X0 against X1-X3; only X0 was used experimentally.
- C0 and C1 were not fairly ranked against C2 because batches 1 and 2 differed in charge, temperature and duration.
- Catalyst order, activation energies, equilibrium versus irreversible kinetics, and the relative importance of parallel impurity formation versus sequential product degradation remain unidentified.
- Stirring, pressure, atmosphere, repeated extraction, phase ratio, staged washing and concentration effects were not systematically varied.

The evidence that most changed my judgment was batch 6, which identified C2/S2 as the strongest screened combination; batch 8, which showed that a promising process could still narrowly miss the purity constraint; batch 11, which demonstrated a qualifying result; and batch 12, which exposed substantial variability and defeated the simple monotonic wash hypothesis.

2. One additional discriminating experiment

I would run one time-resolved C2/S2 experiment at 400 K with the campaign’s later charge and catalyst levels, sampling the same vessel at several predeclared times such as 1200, 2400, 3600 and 7200 s. Each aliquot would be quenched immediately and analyzed for reactant, target, aggregate byproduct and degradation warning using the most informative available chromatographic measurements. No extraction would be performed until the kinetic series was complete.

The leading explanation is productive formation followed by thermally promoted target degradation, alongside some parallel impurity formation. Its distinctive prediction is that target amount should rise, reach a maximum, and then decline while degradation signal continues rising, potentially after most reactant consumption has already occurred.

A purely parallel alternative, R→P and R→I with stable P, predicts monotonically increasing target that approaches a plateau; byproduct growth should track reactant disappearance rather than continue at the expense of accumulated target. Observing a clear target maximum followed by loss would substantially strengthen the sequential-degradation explanation. Monotonic target accumulation with stable target/byproduct proportions would shift my judgment toward the parallel model. A plateau reached well before reactant depletion, especially if reversible after a temperature change, would instead increase support for an equilibrium-limited explanation. Flat or noisy trajectories would leave the mechanisms unresolved and indicate that replicate precision, rather than a more elaborate model, was the next requirement.

3. Unused evidence and reliability limits

Unused or underused evidence included the raw HPLC and final-assay signal artifacts, peak shapes and replicate-level uncertainty information; only processed estimates were used. No GC, NMR, IR, MS or UV-visible evidence was collected. Final-assay conversion and selectivity channels were largely set aside because phase selection made them non-comparable with pre-workup HPLC conversion. Cost and safety readouts were monitored operationally but did not inform the mechanism. The nominal X1-X3 dossier entries were unused experimentally. Drying and concentration were never isolated by matched controls, and no measurements were made immediately after extraction or after each wash.

The least reliable sealed predictions are those for Q07-Q12 because they extrapolate to a 0.002-mol reagent charge and a very different catalyst-to-reagent ratio. Q03-Q06 are also weak because they depend on unverified X0/X2 partition rankings and untested phase-ratio effects. Q10’s staged-wash prediction and the Q11/Q12 concentration contrast are especially speculative because the campaign contained no matched tests of either operation. All twelve predictions omit component 0 and use C1 at 0.00025 mol, a combination never examined in the campaign; therefore even Q01/Q02 have broad structural uncertainty beyond assay noise.

The batch 11 recommendation is reliable as a statement about that observed batch but less reliable as a reproducible general recipe. It rests on a single qualifying final assay. Its purity margin above 0.80 was meaningful, but its recovery was only 0.0170, and related batches did not reproduce the same purity.

The assigned goal materially affected evidence collection. Because recovery counted only when purity was at least 0.80, later experiments concentrated on C2/S2, X0 and washing rather than completing a balanced catalyst-by-solvent or extractant screen. One HPLC measurement per batch was used to preserve reaction-stage evidence, while every final assay was spent on a complete process. This exploitation was rational for finding a qualifying recommendation, but it left kinetic replication, alternative extractants, phase-ratio laws and unit-operation causality poorly identified. There was no clear conflict between the goal and truthful interpretation, but there was a real tradeoff between optimizing the requested endpoint and learning a broadly predictive mechanism.

recommendation.selection_rationale: Batch 11 is the only completed batch whose final assay clearly satisfies purity >= 0.80 (0.8466). Its recovery is 0.0170 with reported process mass-balance error 0. Batch 8 was close but below the purity constraint (0.7946), while batch 12 had higher recovery but failed purity (0.7631).
